description: Figure 3 is a two-panel composite of gray-scale etched microstructure images (metallographic micrographs) of Fe–28Mn–10Al–0.8C low-density steel, each panel carrying a 50 µm scale bar at the lower-left corner and a panel letter at the top-left. Panel (a), the LN steel, is annotated with white arrows and the printed labels "Austenite" and "Ferrite": the austenite matrix is cut by long, straight parallel plates, and the ferrite appears as coarse, dark, elongated stripes decorating austenite grain boundaries, with a few small dark spots. Panel (b), the HN steel, carries the same two printed labels; its structure is visibly finer, with many short thin ferrite laths and fine parallel lamellae inside the austenite grains, plus scattered dark inclusions. No numeric values are printed on either panel; only the 50 µm scale bars and the two phase labels are legible. Read together, the pair makes one argument: nitrogen addition refines the austenite grains and reduces both the size and the amount of boundary ferrite — the microstructural basis, per the citing text, for mean grain sizes of 20.5 µm (LN) versus 12.1 µm (HN) and ferrite area percentages of 5.08% versus 1.84%.

observations.observation: Figure 3 consists of two side-by-side gray-scale etched microstructure images, labelled (a) on the left and (b) on the right, each with a 50 µm scale bar in the lower-left corner.
Both panels carry the printed phase labels 'Austenite' and 'Ferrite', each pointed to by white arrows.
In panel (a) the ferrite appears as coarse, dark, elongated stripe-like bands located at boundaries of the austenite matrix; in panel (b) the ferrite features are visibly smaller and thinner.
Panel (b) contains numerous small dark particles (likely inclusions) scattered in the matrix, whereas panel (a) shows only a few such spots.
No numeric data values, grain-size markers or percentage labels are printed inside either micrograph; only the 50 µm scale bars are quantitative anchors.
The caption states that (a) is the microstructure of LN steel and (b) is that of HN steel.
The citing text states that the mean grain sizes of the LN and HN steels were 20.5 and 12.1 µm, respectively, and that HN steel had finer grains.

The citing text states that ferrites with long parallel stripes formed at austenite boundaries owing to the low precipitation temperature of ferrite, and that ferrite in LN steel was coarser and larger than in HN steel.
The citing text states the area percentage of ferrite was 5.08% in LN steel versus 1.84% in HN steel, attributing this figure to Figure 3.
The citing text states that nitrogen addition promoted grain refinement and increased the austenite area ratio in the Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel.

The citing text states that more fine deformation twins were detected in the austenite grains of the HN steel after forging; the micrographs cannot confirm twin identification at the supplied resolution.
The citing text states that a large number of annealing twins were observed between austenite grains, crossing each other and cutting the matrix to refine the grains, referring to Figure 3.
The citing text links the different ferrite contents seen in these micrographs to the lower yield strength of HN steel (647 MPa) compared with LN steel (685 MPa), citing Table 2 for the values.

subfigures.description: Gray-scale etched microstructure image of the LN steel with a 50 µm scale bar; white arrows and the printed labels 'Austenite' and 'Ferrite' mark the matrix and the coarse, dark, elongated ferrite bands lying along austenite grain boundaries. Long straight parallel plates cross several austenite grains; a few small dark spots are present.

Gray-scale etched microstructure image of the HN steel with a 50 µm scale bar, annotated 'Austenite' and 'Ferrite' by white arrows. The structure is finer than in (a): numerous short thin ferrite laths and fine parallel lamellae (twins) within austenite grains, with small dark particles scattered in the matrix.

identity of the small dark particles/inclusions in panel (b) cannot be determined from the image alone
